subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (for the Minister of Finance) moved
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
that Bill C-139, an Act to amend the Income Tax Act, the Canada Pension Plan, the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Federal PostSecondary Education and Health Contributions Act, 1977 and certain related Acts, be read the third time and passed.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to speak on third reading this morning of what is the most comprehensive reform of our tax system which the Parliament of Canada has seen in the last 20 years. We have had vigorous debate in the House this week. I have said pretty well all I want to say about the motions that have been moved by the Opposition. I would commend those who are interested in the debate to read my responses to the amendments which the Opposition brought forward yesterday.
The Bill, as you know, Mr. Speaker, had its genesis in the June 1987, White Paper on tax reform. This was followed by extensive consultations with taxpayers by myself, by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), by departmental officials, and by the standing committees of the House and the Senate.
I must say, having chaired a parliamentary committee in the first two years of Parliament, that I know how hard Members work on committees. The Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs has worked particularly hard in this session of Parliament, especially so on tax reform. I would like to commend the members of all Parties for the work they have put into this project and the seriousness with which they conducted their deliberations.
I would like to summarize, as we begin third reading, what the objectives were of tax reform in the first place and what we are trying to accomplish. I want to reiterate the momentum we have put behind each objective of tax reform with our various provisions.
First, we believe the fairness of the tax system should be increased. Second, we believe the tax system should encourage competitiveness and growth in jobs. Third, the system should be internally consistent with other Government programs and it should provide a more reliable and balanced source of revenues to finance essential public services. These were our objectives and what we have tried to accomplish. They have been achieved by broadening the base of corporate and personal income tax systems, and by broadening the base we have been able to reduce the rates.
Let us not forget that tax reform reduces rates, and converting personal exemptions and some deductions to credits of course is a major philosophical and practical step forward for fairness in our tax system, which is often overlooked. People say that they would like more deductions or more credits. By shifting exemptions to credits we have made the system fairer and more progressive.
The results of tax reform illustrate how the objectives have been achieved. We are not sort of saying that we are aiming for objectives, but the results prove that the objectives have been reached by shifting more of the tax burden from individuals to corporations and, by lowering tax rates, removing preferences and loopholes in the system, the reforms make the personal income tax system fairer and more progressive.
Let me give you some examples, Mr. Speaker. People ask for results. What are the results of tax reform? How can you prove that it is fair and more equitable? First, net personal income tax revenues to the federal Government will be reduced by $12 billion over the next five years. Second, income taxes will be reduced for 9.7 million, almost 10 million households in this country-85 per cent of all the households-by an average of $490. People will see that difference when they fill in their tax forms.
Lower income Canadians, how have they done? Some
850,000	low-income Canadians will have their income tax reduced to zero or receive refundable credits in 1988.
Income taxes will also be cut for about 1.3 million of the 1.4 million households with at least one person aged 65 and over. About 250,000 elderly Canadians will have their income tax in fact reduced to zero as a result of tax reform. Elderly Canadians in preponderant proportion-1.3 million of the 1.4 million households with at least one person aged 65 or over-will benefit from tax reform.

August 26, 1988
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
Taxes paid by persons with similar incomes and in similar circumstances will vary less after tax reform. One of the great problems that we have in Canada, in the sense of unfairness in the last 20 years, is that people felt that people with the same income were being taxed differently. They did not understand fairness regarding this. A good example is that some people are on salary, some people work for themselves, some people can take advantage of certain preferences and loopholes, and others cannot. We have tried in tax reform, and in a major way have changed this, by putting in place a situation where tax that is paid by persons with similar incomes and in similar circumstances will vary less after tax reform.
A good example-and I constantly had this brought to my attention when we were first elected-is a secretary who works for a large company, London Life, for example, in my home town and did not have the same deductions as somebody who was self-employed. This was becoming a very strong feeling of inequity. The tax reform deals in a major way with that.
Another feeling of inequity that existed was at the corporate tax level. People were saying that it is not just a question of small business and large business; it was industrial sectors. A manufacturing enterprise or a distribution enterprise or a warehousing enterprise pays a certain kind of average tax, but other industrial sectors in Canada such as real estate and financial institutions were in effect paying no tax. There was a perceived sense of unfairness among industrial sectors. For the first time this Government has come to terms with that problem and has made sure that all industrial sectors paid their fair share of taxes. It has not been easy and the finance committee knows this, because it went through the reverberations of this cost.
We have emerged with a package which, when it comes to corporate tax across the industrial sectors, is much more fair. Most taxpayers, as I have said, whose incomes consist primarily of a salary or wages, family allowances or standard pension and retirement revenue, will enjoy tax reductions. It is very important news and we cannot say that often enough.
I said at the opening of my remarks that we were able to reduce taxes. People say: "How can you reduce taxes?" We have done it by removing preferences and loopholes and by broadening the base. Because of base broadening measures through the removal of tax preferences and the conversion of exemptions and reductions to credits, we have produced a more progressive system. This is why 1 objected yesterday to the motion to amend our Bill, arguing for changing the middle income rate from 26 per cent to 23 per cent. Not only would this end up being an $8 billion haemorrhage on the system, but it would be regressive within the middle income bracket, not progressive.
While taxpayers with incomes of less than $15,000 represent 46.7 per cent of total taxpayers, their share of federal tax payable will now decrease from 1.6 per cent to 1.1 per cent. In other words, we are relying on that group.
The lowest income Canadians, the lowest income tax filers, we are relying on them profoundly, but less than we did before
tax reform. The share of federal tax payable by taxpayers with incomes greater than $50,000-these are the wealthier Canadians who represent only 6.3 per cent of the total of taxpayers-will increase from 34.9 per cent to 36.4 per cent. Do not let anybody tell you that we have not increased the burden on the wealthy and decreased it on the lower income groups. In fact, we have increased the burden on the wealthy and decreased the burden on those of lower income.
People ask: "Well, is anybody going to pay more taxes under tax reform". Yes, there are Canadians who will pay more taxes under tax reform. Who are they? These are the ones who have been claiming in the past large special tax preferences or large tax credits. Those with substantial investment income or selfemployment earnings will be subject to the new, fairer expense deduction rules. Those people will be paying more tax. They understand it, but that is part of the base broadening measure in order to lower taxes for other Canadians who are not taking advantage of those preferences.
Corporations will also be paying more taxes. The broadening of the corporate tax base will more than offset the lowering of tax rates. Corporate taxes will increase by 10 per cent or about $5.5 billion over the next five years.
We must remember that tax reform is about fairness on the corporate tax side. This is brought about by broadening the tax base, which allows us to lower tax rates. The result of those two moves, of broadening the base and of lowering the rate, is in fact the production of more corporate tax revenue.
Many more large, profitable corporations will now pay tax as a result of tax reform. With the reduction in tax preferences, the number of profitable corporations not paying tax will be reduced by more than 50 per cent.
Most corporations that do not pay taxes are generally small operations, fledgling operations, that are struggling to keep alive. Through tax reform we are going to be able to find ways to make sure that large, profitable corporations not paying tax will be paying tax. A good example of that, of course, is the taxation of the insurance industry.
Variations of tax paid by different sectors will be reduced prior to tax reform. Average corporate tax rates across industrial sectors range from 14.5 per cent to 24.5 per cent of income on financial statements, and reform has cut this range This is what I was speaking about earlier, the huge differences among industrial sectors on their burden. It is this range, which has been quite wide. It is now going to be narrowed so that it is going to be cut to 15.5 per cent from 22.6 per cent.
Tax reform will also reduce the rate of tax on the return from new investment, strengthening the incentive for firms to invest in profitable ventures. We have heard from the NDP members-and I do not want to ignite a new debate this morning-about how they do not like the capital gains tax. I would think that they would object to me reminding the House that they do not like the capital gains tax being treated differently from income tax.
August 26, 1988

We need in this system, and in just about all industrialized countries, a way to treat capital gains somewhat differently from ordinary income in order to encourage people to take some risks and to take advantage of opportunities that ordinarily would not be taken advantage of. Why? Because we can employ those people and put our economy into a new creative mode with higher employment. That is why there is slight difference in the treatment of capital gains and income tax. We therefore want to make sure that incentive remains.
The over-all financial sector in Canada will pay significantly more in taxes after tax reform, and I would like to speak to that as the Minister of State for Finance, answerable in the House for financial institutions. We have very strong financial institutions. Quite frankly, we have a system which is a model for the rest of the world.
There is a large country in South America with a very weak financial system. There are 360 different banks with just two or three branches each in that country and the people of that country are having great trouble mobilizing capital to lend or to invest in new ventures. The financial system is weak and therefore the economy of that country is very weak.
In Canada, our economy is strong because we have strong and highly efficient capital markets through a highly effective system of financial institutions. As a matter of fact, Canada has the fourth or fifth largest capital market in the world, and it is sustained and made stronger by strong financial institutions.
The strength of financial institutions does not mean exemption from tax. We all know that banks, trust companies, or insurance companies have certain reserves set aside for rainy days or for problems that might occur with people not paying their debts or for insurance claims coming due, but those reserves have to be appropriate from a tax point of view as well. We have attacked this problem. It has been a thorny problem and a difficult problem and we have emerged out the other end with a system that will now be taxing financial institutions fairly, unlike what went before, but not in such a way that will put in jeopardy in any way the great strength of our financial system.
The average tax burden for small firms is unchanged by tax reform while that for large corporations rises. We had a debate yesterday about small business, and there was a motion to decrease the rate on small business still further. The problem with that proposal was that it would also deliver the same benefits at the lower level to large corporations. It would put out of sync the taxation on dividends that flow through a corporation with the taxation of capital gains and the taxation on the corporations themselves. We have tried to align it carefully and have put in place this 12 per cent rate.
The average tax rate for small businesses over all will be 13.5 per cent, a full 7.6 per cent advantage over large firms.
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
Large firms will have an average tax rate of 21.1 per cent. A major part of this relates to the small business deduction which has been maintained and gives a statutory tax for small business that is less than half that of large firms. These are very important steps to keep our small business sector strong and creative. As a result of tax reform, we have secured in place the advantage of small business over large corporations when it comes to taxation.
Canada is a very special country with its huge mining and resource industries. Incentives to the mining industry are very important to this Government. Flow-through shares and the ability to write off all investment against the income of a new mine will be retained, and the average tax rate of the mining sector will remain one of the lowest of all sectors in Canada. I spoke about equity among industrial sectors. There is a sector that we are treating in a preferential way and that is the resource and mining sector. The lower tax rate will more than offset the slightly broader tax base for the oil and gas industry.
All Canadians are concerned about the vitality and dynamism of firms that rely on research and development. Firms engaged in research and development will continue to benefit from one of the most favourable tax regimes for R and D in the industrialized world. Going through OECD arrangements for each country for tax treatment of research and development, one would be hard pressed to find one more generous than the one provided through the tax reform of this Government for research and development in Canada.
Revenue Canada's recent streamlining of the administration of the fully refundable R and D tax credit for small firms is a further useful step forward. A new general anti-avoidance rule will also help prevent abuse of tax avoidance arrangements and new information requirements for investment income and tax shelters will help identify avoidance and evasion.
I will not take much more of the time of the House, but let me relate all of this back to the objectives of the Government as stated by the Minister of Finance when he brought forth the White Paper in June of 1987. He said that in the final analysis, this whole package will be judged on whether we have given to our senior citizens more peace of mind and security, to those in greatest need a sense of a fairer and reduced tax burden, to our young a greater sense of opportunity and hope, and to our working people, more incentive, more stability and more freedom. I think Hon. Members can agree that we have met these objectives.
I would like to say a very special thank you to my colleagues and all members of all Parties who worked hard on the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs which, starting last fall, spent endless hours studying the tax reform package. The thorough review of the members of the committee led to a number of improvements and refinements in the legislation and I know that they are rightly proud of their work.

August 26, 1988
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
[ Translation]
The tax reform proposals were designed to provide Canadians with a more equitable and more comprehensive system that encourages initiative, strengthens competitiveness, growth and job creation and provides a more reliable and balanced source of revenues to finance essential public services.

In conclusion, tax reform comes to terms with two difficult tasks. It makes the system fairer but it is also fiscally responsible. Yesterday during debate, a number of amendments were discussed. Good intentions were behind a number of these amendments, I have no doubt, in order to help certain groups, but I pointed out that the amendments themselves in every case ended up almost contradicting their own objectives because they would interfere in a contradictory way with the rest of tax reform.
Second, I did some mathematics. It would cost almost $9 billion in extra revenue for governments, and that would have the result of putting an additional burden on the Government of Canada to borrow, borrow, borrow. This causes the Government to pay more and more interest on Government borrowings, which in the long run simply burdens generations of those who will have to grow up and pay for the system. With tax reform, we have tried to make it fair, to make it clear, and to make it a system of hope for all Canadians, but also to be fiscally responsible.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before starting the comments I wanted to make on third reading of this Bill, I would like to comment very briefly on what was said by the Minister of State (Finance) (Mr. Hockin). First of all, I must say I was very disappointed the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) did not take part in the debate himself and left that responsibility to his Minister of State. This is no reflection on the competence and sense of responsibility of the Minister of State (Finance), but since the debate is about tax reform which the Minister claims has taken up the majority of his time since he was appointed, I wonder why he is not taking part in the debate and entrusted a junior Minister with the task of informing Canadians about the various aspects of this Bill.
In any case, the Minister of State (Finance) repeated the same kind of rhetoric the Minister of Finance gave us when he brought down his Budget. Unfortunately, this repetitive rhetoric fails to reflect the substance of the legislation. That is unfortunate and that is the whole problem.
Earlier, the Minister commended members of the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs of the House of Commons, and in fact all three Parties, for having worked so hard, both at public hearings and when drafting a report that was later tabled in the House. Of course we appreciate those kind words, Mr. Speaker, but for over three months we heard testimony from witnesses, both before and after the Finance Minister's report was tabled. We received a very clear message from most witnesses and it was: The Government's rhetoric is
at odds with the contents of the Bill. We heard this from senior citizens, businessmen, the mining industry, the insurance sector and from practically all groups that appeared before the Committee, explaining that they agreed with the principle but were against certain aspects. In fact, Mr. Speaker, it became a farce. Every time we received a brief, it said: We agree with the principles, we urge the Government to continue in the direction it proposes, but finally, the brief would shoot down the tax reform paper.
The Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs made any number of recommendations over ninety if I am not mistaken, and practically none were accepted. It got to the point that even Conservative Members on the Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs who examined the Bill were tempted many times to vote against certain provisions. As my colleague from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) said last night, it was because of subsequent pressure that certain decisions were reversed.
Mr. Speaker, once again, the Minister has served up the same rhetoric we heard from the Minister of Finance, the rhetoric that does not coincide with the Bill and the tax measures it contains. He talked about lower taxes, as the Minister did, but of course he refrained from pointing out that these adjustments don't even compensate for the tax increases we had before. I have often explained tax reform by comparing it to a woman whose handbag is stolen by a thief in a park. A few minutes later, the thief gives the woman her purse back, after taking all the money, and he expects the woman to be grateful! That is something like what they have done. They increased taxes for four years and on the eve of the election, they lower them by about 10 per cent. Big deal! They claim to be the saviours who are bringing fairness to the tax system.
Mr. Speaker, today we are beginning the final stage of consideration of the tax reform Bill. I do not intend to repeat all the arguments that I developed in Committee and yesterday when the report was considered. The Minister, in referring to these amendments, just told us that it would cost a fortune! But the Minister knows very well that at the report stage, we cannot present amendments that are as complex as tax reform itself, because the Chair would reject them. What we were trying to show with these amendments was the inequity of this tax reform, which should have eliminated this unfairness towards different population groups and brought a little more justice to the various classes of taxpayers.
For example, I proposed full indexation of refundable tax credits for children and for blind or disabled people. Obviously, I see this as a matter of social justice, for two reasons: the financial problems families have and the declining birth rate in this country. Therefore, a way had to be found not to penalize families. The cost was not exorbitant. As for the disabled, it seems to me that the tax credit for them ... if there is one group in society that deserves to be protected from the ravages of inflation, it is this one! That was suggested by many groups. But the Minister and Government Members said no, it was too expensive.
August 26, 1988

I will get back later to the issue of cost and the promises made by the Conservative Government. Why do they have money for promises and none for providing a fair tax system?
The Minister says that some of our measures would cost billions of dollars. Yesterday, for instance, I suggested that the tax credit that would replace personal exemptions be made refundable for people on very low incomes, the reason being that people with high incomes can take advantage of 100 per cent of the credit, but if a person has no taxable income, he loses out on the tax credit.
The Minister ridiculed my suggestion, saying that the Government would have to give a refundable tax credit to every new-born child. Mr. Speaker, that is the silliest thing I ever heard and it is a deliberate attempt to trivialize the purpose of this amendment. I realize that it is only fair for Members on the other side of the Elouse to try and shoot down the arguments of their opponents, but for a Minister of Finance, for a Minister of State (Finance) to put this kind of interpretation on an amendment and calculate the cost at billions of dollars is totally irresponsible.
So despite the hard work by the Finance Committee and by Liberal Members on that Committee-we tabled the fifteen amendments we considered yesterday-despite all our hard work, the Government did not see fit to accept those amendments. If it had, it would have been possible to improve the Bill and bring it more into line with the Government's objectives.
Mr. Speaker, I think we should see tax reform within the broader context of the fiscal strategy we have seen unfolding in recent years.
There is always a tendency on the part of the Government- fair is fair, I suppose-to put the spotlight on tax reform so as better to hide the tax increases it introduced in recent years. If you put this reform in its proper perspective, we see that despite tax reform, over the past four years Canadian taxpayers have been hit by tax increases that are the biggest and most massive we have known in our parliamentary history.
Mr. Speaker, 1 will start with indirect taxes. When I give you the figures, I am going to give the rates and amounts the Minister gave us, which do not allow for the effects, if any, of economic growth.
For instance, since 1984, the Conservative Government increased federal sales tax from 9 per cent to 12 per cent. That decision alone will, in 1988-89, raise $3 billion more in revenue than the Government would have collected in federal sales tax if there had been no increase, and I am not talking about any effects of economic growth or growth in consumption but only about the rate. In one year, as a result of successive increases in sales tax, the Government collects $3 billion more, and I am referring to 1988-89.
The Government also expanded sales tax to cover candy, soft drinks, certain pharmaceutical products, snacks and so
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
forth. On an annual basis, for 1988-89 this change in the sales tax structure provides the Minister of Finance with $400 million more in revenue. The excise tax on a litre of gas was increased 5 cents, which means that for 1988-89 alone, the result is additional revenue for the Minister of Finance totalling $2,225,000.
The Minister of Finance has repeatedly raised taxes and excise tax on alcohol and tobacco. For 1988-89 alone, the result of the policies of the Minister of Finance has been to take an extra $735 million out of taxpayers' pockets. I take all those figures, Mr. Speaker, from the budgets tabled by the Minister of Finance.
By imposing a 10 per cent tax on long distance telephone calls and cable television service, the Minister is taking another billion dollars from the taxpayers' pockets in the current fiscal year. The Minister raised the tax on paint, wallpaper and air transport by $60 million a year.
If one adds all this up for the 1988-89 fiscal year alone, without factoring in economic growth, the effect of the Government's policies to increase tax rates is to collect $7.4 billion more from the taxpayers in this fiscal year.
The sales tax had been increased from 9 per cent to 12 per cent; the excise tax on gasoline by five cents per litre. Taxes on tobacco and alcohol have been increased during the last four years. There was a 10 per cent tax on long distance calls, costing Canadian taxpayers $1 billion. When we add it together, in the fiscal year 1988-89 the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) collected, just from the increased rate of taxation on indirect taxes, $7.4 billion of new money.
Let us consider the direct tax system, particularly the personal income tax. The numbers I will give to the House come directly from the budget speech. I did not invent them. The fact is that since 1986, personal income tax has been deindexed one year after the another. This means that in this fiscal year the Government will collect $1.8 billion of new taxes from personal income tax. This is not due to a change in rate but as a result of partial deindexation of our tax system. It is a hidden tax because the Minister does not announce those changes every year.
In the first year it amounted to $650 million; the second year it was $1.2 billion; and this year it is $1.8 billion. It has an accumulative effect year after year. In 1988-89, the Minister will collect close to $2 billion more in taxes due to partial deindexation.
The Government has eliminated some of the fiscal advantage that the family received in the past and, as a result, will collect $600 million more in 1988-89.

August 26, 1988
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, the Government imposed a general 3 per cent surtax which was to be temporary, but which has been in effect for several years and now seems to be embedded in the system. This too provides the Government with more money, so that the total amount of new money that the Government has obtained not from economic growth but from changes in tax rates and fields of taxation and from partial deindexation of the system is $4 billion.
Mr. Speaker, if I take the increases in sales tax, which in 1988-89 amount to $7.4 billion, and add the increases in personal income taxes of $4 billion, I come out with a total of $11 billion in direct taxes for only one year. I did not add up the figures for 1986, 1987 and 1988, but for the 1988-89 fiscal year alone, the increases in direct and indirect taxes were $11 billion.

For the fiscal year 1988-89 alone, the Minister of Finance will collect from the Canadian taxpayer $11 billion more just through the increase in the tax rate in the field of taxation. It is not as a result of an increase in the economy.
Let us examine those figures and take into account certain fiscal advantages coming from the fiscal reform. While the tax breaks are less, let us be generous and assume that they will be $2 billion. If we take $11 billion of increases minus $2 billion in tax breaks just before the election, there is a net amount of $9 billion in new taxes. When one considers that there is a deficit of $28 billion, without those tax increases the real deficit of the Government would be $37 billion. One of the Government's main campaign platforms from the Minister of Finance was deficit control. He said that the deficit would be solved, not by tax increases but by better management of public affairs. It is really a farce.

Adding up the $7 billion in indirect taxes and the $4 billion in direct taxes, and taking account of the positive effects of tax reform on some sectors, one sees that the Minister of Finance has collected $9 billion net more in taxes in 1988-89 alone; comparing that to the $28-billion deficit, one realizes that were it not for massive tax increases, the deficit would be $36 or $37 billion. For a Government that boasts of its good management of public finances, this is really laughable.
Mr. Speaker, consider as well that economic growth is due to the world economic situation and that the Minister of Finance clearly said in his budget speech, perhaps a little naively, in the first part of his speech, that the economic recovery in Canada had begun before the Conservatives took power. If we were in a more stable economic situation, we would have a deficit of over $40 billion. I want to point out to the Minister of Finance that his management of public finances has been completely irresponsible and that the promises he made to Canadian taxpayers... I still hear the Finance Minister and the Prime Minister talking to us about this solemn promise not to raise taxes, that the deficit would instead be controlled by reducing expenses. Well, as in other cases, these promises have not been kept. Not only were they
not held, but the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister chose a direction directly opposite to their commitments.
Mr. Speaker, returning to tax reform proper and the legislation now before us, I would say that one feature of those tax increases, in addition to being the most massive in Canadian history, because no other government had succeeded in a four-year period in raising taxes to such a dramatic extent-the worst part of the matter is that most of those tax increases were hidden by the indirect effect of de-indexation and by increases in indirect taxes that the taxpayer, the consumer does not see when he buys goods from the store. Because the Government preferred to raise indirect taxes, the invisible ones, those that are hidden in the price of goods, rather than direct taxes. Even when the Government increases direct taxes, it does so in a secretive, devious way. This is why, instead of raising rates directly, it went through partial deindexation.
Mr. Speaker, one of the major failures of that tax reform is that it did not reach the goals set by the Minister in his White Paper, neither did it meet the goals referred to by the Minister of State (Finance) each time he rises. It is one thing to recite principles and state objectives, but when bills are introduced that fly in the face of those principles, Mr. Speaker, we wonder whether they are being naive or quite simply hypocritical, whether they are trying to deceive electors. For instance, looking at the major questions that might be asked on the matter of fairness, I am not the only one to suggest this, Mr. Speaker. True I have been stating this ad nauseam since the beginning, because this tax reform is structured in a way that is unfair to middle-income people, to families and to some extent to low-income senior citizens.
I would like to know how the Government explains away a number of concerns raised by taxpayers, by associations that appeared before the Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs. I would like to refer to those questions that were raised and that I am also raising to the Government and the Minister of Finance.
How does the Government explain that Canadian middle-income earners will pay $1,200 more in taxes this year than they did in 1984, while Canadians whose earnings are greater than $117,000 a year will pay $3,500 less in taxes? How does the Government explain the inequity of low income earners paying more and higher income earners paying much less?
Why has the Government abolished the $1,000 deduction for investment income which is frequently used by middle income earners and by old age pensioners, while granting an exemption of $100,000 in capital gains for the benefit of the wealthy? Why this double standard? Why do we abolish exemptions that help the middle class and senior citizens, on the one hand, and give to the rich people an exemption of capital gains?
August 26, 1988

Why did the Government not follow the suggestion made by the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs and abolish the capital gains exemption with a formula that would take inflation into account? Why did the Government set aside this proposal? Why does it have money to give capital gains exemptions to the rich and does not have the money to keep the $1,000 interest deduction for senior citizens?
How does the Government explain that benefits which flow from the child care expenses deduction or those from the RRSP contributions are greater for higher income Canadians? Why were these deductions not converted into tax credits which would have contributed to improving the equity of the tax system and the usefulness of these programs?
Why has the tax rate for small manufacturing companies increased from 10 per cent to 12 per cent when the objective of tax reform is to reduce the tax rate?
Why did the Government give a break to large companies? It seems to have the money to do that, but the Government increases the tax rate for small manufacturing companies from 10 per cent to 12 per cent. Not only did the Government increase the tax rate for small businesses from 10 per cent to 12 per cent, but it went back on the promise the Minister made in this House to bring down that rate to 8 per cent. Not only did the Minister not respect the commitment he made in this House to the small business sector, but he did the opposite and increased the rate from 10 per cent to 12 per cent.
How does the Government explain that some 60,000 profitable businesses will continue to pay no taxes after tax reform? How does the Government explain that the tax system has not been simplified? According to the report of the committee on finance, the tax system will be more complex when the objective was to simplify it.
How does the Government explain its decision to base its tax system on credit which can be easily and fully used by taxpayers in the middle income or higher income brackets but which cannot be fully used by lower income taxpayers? Why are they not made refundable? Why was this opportunity not used to set the stage for a true minimum guaranteed income? Where is the equity in this legislation?

As I asked a moment ago in English, Mr. Speaker, how does one explain the Government's decision to do away with the $1,000 deduction? First, alleging that it is too costly, they scrap the $1,000 investment income deduction of older Canadians, then they turn around and allow a $100,000 capital gains tax exemption. What is the rationale behind the fact that, through direct taxes and lower family benefits, the average income taxpayer with children has to pay back to the federal Government 31 per cent of any salary increase, whereas the very wealthy taxpayer's repayment is only 29 per cent? Is that fair? Why would family assistance programs be eroded every year as a result of partial de-indexation when Canada's birth rate happens to be among the lowest in the world? Where is the fairness in the approach of the Minister of
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
Finance? Would someone tell me why the Government chose to abolish the deduction for dependent children aged 19 to 21 precisely when they undertake costly post-graduate studies?
Mr. Speaker, not only does the Government disallow the child deduction even for those aged 19 to 21 and still attending school, but it also eliminates the option a mother living alone might otherwise have had to claim her 19-year-old child as spouse for tax purposes. This has always been possible under our system. In the case of a widow or the case of a singleparent family it was possible to claim the so-called equivalent to married credit. The Conservative Government has now struck out that provision in the case of children over 18 so that a family whose children are attending a post-secondary institution or going to university can no longer claim the child tax credit. And a widow or a single-parent family will no longer be able to use a university-attending dependent child to claim the equivalent to married deduction in the tax return.
How are we to explain this inequity? How are we to explain the Government decision to base its tax system on credits which can be easily and fully used by middle and higher-income taxpayers, but which cannot be used by lower-income taxpayers?
Mr. Speaker, it is clear that if you do not have enough income to pay income tax, you cannot benefit from this tax credit. This seems to me as clear as day! It seems to me also that if the Government had wanted to be a little imaginative it might at least have allowed this class of citizens to use and benefit from the tax credit system just as their fellow citizens in higher-income brackets do.
When the Minister of State (Finance) mockingly suggested that perhaps the Government should grant tax credit to newborn babies, he showed both his ignorance and unwillingness to make our tax system more equitable.
How are we to explain that small businessmen, as well as self-employed workers and contractors will no longer be allowed to claim a full deduction for entertainment expenses on their income tax returns, even those who have to go outside their towns or villages where their head-offices or main working locations are situated.
The situation is such that if you were to go and work for a corporation, or if you are self-employed and living, say, in Quebec, and decided to come and attend a seminar in Montreal to improve your skills or seek more expertise in attending work groups, you could not use 100 per cent of your hotel or restaurant expenses against your income, even if these expenses are directly related to your business operations.
I suggest it is alltogether unfair. These expenses will be limited from now on to only 80 per cent. We know that will result in all sorts of complication and encourage these people into making income tax returns which are not true to reality, because the Minister of Finance has failed to demonstrate openmindedness, and both listen to and understand the recommendations made by all these self-employed workers.

August 26, 1988
That is the reason why we, on this side of the Elouse, declare that this Tory Government has failed in its effort to carry out a true tax reform, and that the Minister and his Tory colleagues are making claims which are not at all reflected in the Bill before us. I suggest that the Government did not avail itself of this opportunity to . ..

subtopic: NATURAL RESOURCES
NATURAL RESOURCES
subsubtopic: PROPOSED LEGISLATION TO PROTECT WATER RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-156, the Bill to protect Canadian water resources, which was tabled yesterday by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan), is not comprehensive, or coherent. It is a hastily put together, incomplete, and hollow response to public pressure. For example, because the Bill only prohibits the increase of water flowing across the international boundary, it will not prevent the export of water by tankers.
Cabinet has powers to allow the export or diversion of water without an environmental impact assessment. Cabinet can also remove restrictions on the quantity of water that can be exported without consultation with Parliament, according to Clause 13.
The offences under the legislation are bizarre. Can you visualize, Mr. Speaker, someone being fined or imprisoned for diverting a river? Would it be after diversion, before, or when cutting the ribbon?
Finally, and most important, this Bill makes no difference to the free trade agreement, confirming the fact that this Bill cannot stop the export of water under the free trade agreement.

subtopic: U.S.S.R.-TREATMENT OF UKRAINIANS
U.S.S.R.-TREATMENT OF UKRAINIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the announcement of the 1988 version of glasnost and
perestroika, many have held high expectations for change in the Soviet Union. However, those expectations continue to be dashed and betrayed.
On August 7, Reverend Michajlo Hawryliw was arrested in Ukraine for serving a Catholic mass. He was sentenced to 15 days at an internal KGB prison in Rozhniatiw. Reverend Petro Zeleny was fined 100 rubles for serving the holy liturgy.
In Lviv, Ivan Makar is serving time in the Hapaev Street Prison for his part in the July 7 demonstration in front of Ivan Franko's monument, where thousands of demonstrators, in the spirit of the supposed reforms, asked for the legalization of the Ukrainian Catholic Church, proclaiming Urkainian the official language in the schools and erecting a monument to the victims of Stalin's terror.
Once again we are reminded that we must not confuse Soviet promises with Soviet reality.
I call upon the Government of Canada to issue a formal protest to Soviet officials for their continued blatant violations of fundamental religious and human rights in Ukraine.

subtopic: UNION NEGOTIATIONS-POSITION OF PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
UNION NEGOTIATIONS-POSITION OF PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to draw to the attention of the House the problems that members of the Professional Institute of the Public Service and its leadership have been having in dealing with the President of the Treasury Board (Miss Carney) and with the Government.
This is a union which is not militant. It is a union whose

In 1984, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised that his Party looked forward to working "constructively" with the Professional Institute of the Public Service as they negotiated solutions to many complex Public Service issues.
Since the new Minister took office this spring, apart from one reception which she gave for Public Service union leaders, she has refused to arrange any constructive and reasonable meetings with those Public Service unions, including the head of PIPS. She has told them that she does not want to meet if collective bargaining is going on. However, the fact is that collective bargaining has been frustrated for a year with PIPS members and leadership on a master bargaining contract, which means that the President of the Treasury Board would never meet them.

August 26, 1988

Her office has told the President of PIPS, Iris Craig, that she is either too busy or too tired to meet with those representatives. If the President of the Treasury Board is too tired, then she should resign and let someone else have the job.

subtopic: SUPPORT FOR CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT
SUPPORT FOR CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are more than 840,000 small businesses in Canada. Over
1,200,000	jobs have been created since the election in 1984 of the Conservative Government. Many of those positions have been created by small businesses.
The President of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business maintains that small businesses view free trade as being advantageous for growth and future prosperity.
This week I visited numerous small businesses in my riding of Edmonton East. All the small business people with whom I spoke endorsed free trade with the United States.
One company, Titan Foundry Ltd., stated that the elimination of the 7 per cent American tariff would immediately double exports to the U.S. market.
It is clear that most small businesses in Edmonton want to see the free trade agreement with the United States become a reality.

subtopic: FUTURE OF FRANCOPHONES IN CANADA
FUTURE OF FRANCOPHONES IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since our Progressive Conservative Government is in power, we have realized the urgency that Canada be better recognized internationally as a French-speaking country, since an educated, intelligent and enterprising French-speaking population represent almost one third of the Canadian population.
What have we done for that in concrete terms? First, we advocated French-speaking Summits, as the one in Quebec City last year. Second, we have passed Bill C-72 on the official languages to protect, maintain and promote the Frenchspeaking minority in Canada.
Next week, that is September 2 to 9, the International Association of French-speaking parliamentarians, of which I am an executive member, will meet in Quebec City, Pointe-
Au-Pic and Ottawa, as an ad hoc follow-up commission after the French-speaking Summit of Quebec City.
Mr. Speaker, those are the concrete measures that our Governement has taken to support the French-speaking people of Canada and of Quebec.

subtopic: SITUATION IN SOUTHERN NEW BRUNSWICK-REQUEST FOR MINISTERIAL ACTION

speechtext: Mr Fernand Robichaud (Westmoreland-Kent):	Mr. Speaker, for some months now, people in southern New Brunswick have been very concerned about their Unemployment Insurance benefits. The eligibility period has been extended from 10 to 16 weeks in an area where often unemployment adjusted rates nearly reach or are even higher than 30 per cent. The only reaction from the Minister to this serious problem has been to announce a full review of all economic regions. Again another review! Why did the Minister choose this course of action? Many studies have already been conducted. This problem has been examined quite a few times. The Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration submitted a unanimous report on unemployment insurance. That report suggested as a first recommendation the establishment of a standard eligibility period of 10 insurable employment weeks. The Minister has all the facts at hand. Time has come for her to act, and right now, so that people from southern New Brunswick be treated with some justice.

subtopic: WINNIPEG-STORAGE OF PCBS IN RAILWAY BOXCAR
WINNIPEG-STORAGE OF PCBS IN RAILWAY BOXCAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the tragic incident at Saint-Basile-le-Grand has alerted us all to the dangers of PCBs. We find now that in Winnipeg there is a boxcar with PCBs in it sitting in the city of Winnipeg. It is right beside an actively used railway track. There is no fencing. This boxcar is inadequately secured.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), has taken the time to see this site and talk to officials involved. He is looking into the matter.
The provincial government has said that it is not its responsibility. It is the responsibility of the federal Government. Environment Canada says that it needs the guidelines of the department. We need more than guidelines to protect us from these environmental hazards. We need regulations.

August 26, 1988
As a first measure we ought to be inquiring into the whole question of PCBs across the country, where they are, under what conditions they are presently stored, and what standards are needed so that people can be assured that they are safe.

subtopic: CANADA POST CORPORATION-ADOPTION OF COMPULSORY ARBITRATION ADVOCATED

speechtext:
Mir. Ross Belsher (Fraser Valley East): Mr. Speaker, Canadians do not like strikes. In an article in yesterday's The Gazette William Johnson made the following observations regarding the postal strike:
"Postal strikes are absurd. The government creates a monopoly of mail delivery which makes the entire population vulnerable; then it gives a few thousand post office workers the right to stab the public.
Strikes in the post office are not an economic tug-of-war in which both sides to the dispute must take into account the survival of the company being struck.
Post office strikes are political strikes. The damage is not done to the employer; it is done to the public.
In his recently published book, A Public Purpose, Tom Kent, a policy adviser to the Pearson Government, refers to collective bargaining and the right to strike. He makes this comment:
"The cause of subsequent trouble lay not in public service collective bargaining, which was inevitable, but in the broadness of the right to strike and the carelessness of bureaucratic expansionism that followed. Before the end, the Pearson government was beginning to take fright at the prospects.
In his article Johnson went on to state:
"To restore labour peace and restore true collective bargaining, some form of compulsory arbitration must be imposed on the post office.
I whole-heartedly endorse the above views.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT- CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD
CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT- CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Wheat Board has been a valuable asset for Prairie farmers. Under the terms of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement it will continue to benefit Canada. The agreement will not require changes in the Wheat Board marketing system, nor will it require disclosure of Wheat Board prices or other commercial information that could benefit competitors. If anything, the Board's ability to market grain will be enhanced.
As well, with the requirement under free trade for end-use certificates for imported grain, the integrity of our grain system will not be compromised. What the agreement does is create tremendous opportunities for Canada's grain producers
in the U.S. market. Commodity groups, such as the canola producers and the Western Canadian Wheat Growers Association, agree.
The opponents of the free trade agreement will have a tough time convincing Canada's grain farmers.

subtopic: PROPOSED ACQUISITION OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES
PROPOSED ACQUISITION OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night in the town of Milton the Minister for National Defence (Mr. Beatty), in his usual courteous manner, referred to the Member for Hamilton East as a dog. I can tell the Minister one thing. I would rather be a dog than a Tory.

subtopic: POSITION OF CANADIAN MEDICAL ASSOCIATION
POSITION OF CANADIAN MEDICAL ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at recent conventions both the United Church of Canada and the Canadian Medical Association reaffirmed the position that a decision regarding abortion is a medical decision that should be made by a woman and her doctor after all options are seriously considered.
The Canadian Medical Association also recommended medical standards for counselling, informed choice, medical, surgical, and nursing procedures, and follow-up care. Health care insurance should cover costs of medically required services, including counselling, early diagnosis of pregnancy, and early access, across Canada, to abortion should be encouraged.
August 26, 1988

The medical profession has provided an important contribution in clarifying abortion as a medical procedure with standards for practice and respect for differing personal views. The Canada Health Act must ensure fair access across Canada.
The best manner in which to reduce unwanted pregnancies is prevention; greater emphasis on effective and safe birth control, and government funding for family planning are essential. Women and doctors make responsible and moral decisions, and there is no evidence to the contrary.

subtopic: EXPLOSION IN PCB WAREHOUSE AT SAINT-BASILE-LE-GRAND-GOVERNMENT FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE

speakeroldname: Mr. Richard Grise (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: EXPLOSION IN PCB WAREHOUSE AT SAINT-BASILE-LE-GRAND-GOVERNMENT FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since last Tuesday, my constituents in Chambly, and especially in Saint-Basile-le-Grand and Saint-Bruno, have been going through an emergency crisis.
The area was the scene of the worst-ever environmental disaster in Quebec. A PCB warehouse caught fire, and several thousands of residents in my constituency had to evacuate their homes.
As soon as I heard about the fire, I rushed to the scene. I stayed until the next morning ensuring all concerned of my full co-operation.
When such a disaster strikes, it is comforting to see the joint efforts by authorities to ensure the security of the people. For example, when 1 was asked to contact the CFB Saint-Hubert, they immediately sent a fire truck specially equipped for this kind of accident.
I want to mention the tireless efforts and hard work of the firefighters in my constituency of Chambly. I also want to congratulate them for their courage.
Our Government also took their responsabilities, as is the rule in this kind of situation. Yesterday, on the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) request, the Transport Minister (Mr. Bouchard, the Environment Minister (Mr. McMillan), the Member for Vercheres (M. Danis) and myself went to the scene of the accident to guarantee the population our support.
In fact, the Prime Minister has announced that our Government will join others in offering financial assistance to the residents of Chambly. Last night, following a request by Environment Canada, a sophisticated mobile laboratory was sent to evaluate the air inside the homes. This service is paid for by the federal Government.
Mr. Speaker, I want to assure the population of my constituency of Chambly, of Quebec and of Canada that our
Government is doing all we can to help the victims and to make sure such a tragedy never happens again.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POSITION OF FARMERS
CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POSITION OF FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on August 24, a press release from the Canadian Agricultural Policy Alliance strongly endorsed the trade agreement with the United States. This group, which represents farmers all across Canada, has expressed strong support for the free trade agreement.
Past CCA president, Stan Wilson, stated: "Contrary to the view expressed by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, it is clear that the large majority of farmers would welcome freer access to the large and prosperous U.S. market". The Canadian Agricultural Policy Alliance represents grain, oilseed, hog, beef, and cattle producers from all parts of Canada.
The United States is already Canada's largest market for farm commodities, and it is becoming more important as other countries reduce their purchases.
The members feel the removal of tariffs and quotas, the improved method of dealing with disputes, and the process for resolving non-tariff barriers are all positive developments for Canadian farmers. This is especially true for the sectors interested in selling processed, high quality products into the large and sophisticated U.S. market.
Mr. Wilson concluded: "There is no doubt freer access to the U.S. market will be beneficial to the large majority of Canadian farmers. With the decline of traditional markets for grains and oilseeds, the very survival of large sectors of Canadian agriculture could well depend on secure access to the large and prosperous North American market. All farm groups should be working together to that end".

subtopic: BOYCOTT OF CONTAMINATED CALIFORNIA GRAPES
BOYCOTT OF CONTAMINATED CALIFORNIA GRAPES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no question that the pervasive use of toxic pesticides by many countries is the greatest threat posed to the health of people, and to the world environment.
A plea for reduced pollution and wiser world economic development always seems to fall on deaf ears, whether they be governments or the private sector, which show little remorse in gambling peoples' lives and health for the sake of the almighty dollar.
Eating food or drinking water contaminated with toxic residue has resulted in deaths, in cancers, and in birth defects.
It is shocking to read that the U.S. Government has estimated that, of 600 active ingredients used as insecticides, only 10 per cent have been studied enough to form an adequate opinion of their health risks.
However, it is gratifying to see some light at the end of the tunnel. More than one thousand labour, community, consumer, and health organizations, including the City of Toronto, and the Ontario Public Health Association, have endorsed the boycott of insecticide contaminated grapes from California. More action and leadership along this line is needed if we are ever to eliminate this scourge of contamination from our food products.

subtopic: DISMANTLING OF SPEAKER'S CORNER
DISMANTLING OF SPEAKER'S CORNER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, correctly spelling Prime Minister Wilfrid Laurier's first name is one of the smaller challenges confronting students of Canadian history.
The National Capital Commission has finally been forced to recognize that the spelling on the plaque placed at Speaker's Corner on the Sparks Street Mall is wrong.
I expect that you are as shocked as I am, Mr. Speaker, that the NCC's response to this discovery is not to replace the plaque with a corrected version but to dismantle the Speaker's Corner.
The Speaker's Corner was, after all, originally unveiled by the Speaker of the House of Commons and the Mayor of
Ottawa, now also a worthy colleague in this debating Chamber the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar).
The NCC Director of Communications blamed Murphy's Law for the original spelling mistake. However, the NCC's decision to remove Speaker's Corner this fall surely gives new meaning to the corollary of Murphy's Law-Murphy was an optimist!

subtopic: INCREASING INTEREST RATES
INCREASING INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, how many times have we seen the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), rise in this House and tell Canadians how the Tory Government was responsible for lowering interest rates while the trained Tory seals, surfers, and book-ends were cheering and applauding?
Well, Mr. Speaker, if one can take credit for lowering interest rates, then one has to take credit for increasing interest rates. As you know, Mr. Speaker, I always give credit where credit is due.
The Government cannot only blow its own horn when it feels that things are going its way. Can we expect both the Prime Minister, and the Minister of Finance, to rise in the House today and say to Canadians: "If the interest rates are higher and you need to dig deeper in your pockets, you can say, 'thank you Brian, thank you Michael, we did it for you'"?

subtopic: ECOLOGICAL ACCIDENTS
ECOLOGICAL ACCIDENTS
subsubtopic: SAINT-BASILE-LE-GRAND-REQUEST THAT POPULATION AFFECTED BE BETTER INFORMED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the fire at a PCB warehouse in Saint-Basile-le-Grand near Montreal is becoming one of the worst environmental tragedies in Canada's recent history. Would the Minister of the Environment or the Minister now acting on his behalf tell us what advice his experts have given him concerning the negative impact of this tragic incident on the health of the residents of Saint-Basile and surrounding areas? What steps has the Government taken to give the residents precise and clear information on their situation? All sorts of rumours are circulating. What is the possible impact of toxic fallout on the health of pregnant women? Are vegetables safe to eat, is milk from cows grazing in contaminated fields safe to drink? Those are the kind of questions people are asking and I am sure the Minister would be willing to share the advice from his experts with this House and, through television, with all Canadians. This would surely help and reassure the people involved.
August 26, 1988

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE
ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Justice. I recently saw articles in the newspaper saying that alleged murderers hope to obtain refugee status in Canada and thus avoid the law of their own country. Charles Ng came to Canada in 1985, to escape the authorities in California and has not yet been extradited despite a formal request from the U.S.

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE
subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT CHARLES NG BE EXTRADITED TO UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question. We have to keep in mind the distinction between immigration law dealing with deportation, and refugee status and the extradition process which operates according to treaties between countries.
With respect to Mr. Ng, officials in my Department have been working closely with American officials on this very sensitive issue. A formal request was received on, I believe, November 3, 1987. An arrest warrant was initiated by officials of my Department on behalf of the Americans on November 17. Before the matter came up for a hearing the fugitive made an application for adjournment of the case to the fall of 1988 on the basis that he had not had sufficient time to prepare material for the case. We vigorously opposed this but the court ordered the matter set forward to the fall.

August 26, 1988
Oral Questions
I can assure the Hon. Member that the position of counsel acting on behalf of the Americans continues to be that the case should proceed at the earliest possible date. Member it will be given the appropriate attention.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when you saw it was eleven o'clock and time for Question Period, I had finished part of my speech, pointing out that increases in indirect taxes and income tax by the Conservative Government during the past four years had resulted in additional revenues of $11 billion for 1988-89 alone. I also said that, allowing for certain adjustments made as a result of tax reform, the net increase in taxes resulted in additional revenues for the Government of almost $9 billion for 1988-89. In fact, without these massive tax increases, the Conservative Government's deficit would be between 36 and 37 billion dollars, and this after six years of economic recovery!
Mr. Speaker, the facts I just mentioned, which are supported by the Budgets brought down by the Minister of Finance
(Mr. Wilson) in the last four years, are a clear indication that this Government failed to act on the commitments it made to Canadians. Both the present Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised they would not increase taxes and would reduce the deficit by cutting expenditures. That is not what they did, and without the massive tax increases, the Conservative Government's deficit would be $4 or $5 billion more than it was during the last full year of the Liberal Government's administration, a Government this Conservative Party has loudly criticized.
Mr. Speaker, in concluding, I would like to comment on two aspects-first of all on the impact that certain tax reform provisions may have on economic growth-and I will then finish my speech on a more general note.
Mr. Speaker, this Government which claims to encourage capital formation-research, development, investment in industrial and commercial sectors that create jobs-has introduced tax reform proposals that are likely to discourage high-risk investment. The Government's goal should have been to encourage and promote investment in the higher-risk sectors of research and development, including specific technologies developed by university researchers and research centres. This is vital to the long-term health of our economy.
Instead of promoting capital formation and investment, the Minister of Finance has implemented measures that will make the task of prospective investors even more difficult and hazardous.
For instance, why will capital gains, from now on, be taxed more heavily than dividend income?
Mr. Speaker, the 1971 tax reform stemmed from the study of the Carter Commission which had produced a white paper paving the way for public consultation leading to the inclusion of a new element in the 1971 reform, the capital gains tax. Capital gains being subject to inflation it was decided to tax one half of these gains at the taxpayer's marginal rate. Well, Mr. Speaker, we all agree that worldwide conditions have evolved in recent years and countries like England and the United States changed their approach. For one thing, the British chose to tax capital gains at 100 per cent, but they came up with an indexation formula under which the tax would apply only to real gains and not to those due to inflation. I think this is a very commendable approach and, in our context, I would agree that capital gains become fully taxable if we were to devise that kind of indexation formula.
As a matter of fact our own finance committee made that suggestion to the Government when they said: If you are not prepared to proceed with full reform and tax all capital gains while implementing an indexation formula to account for inflation, you should settle for only two thirds instead of three quarters, otherwise you would be taxing capital gains at higher marginal rates than those applicable to the dividends people get from their investments.
August 26, 1988

Why did the Minister completely ignore this unanimous recommendation from the finance committee and similar views expressed by the many observers who gave evidence before the committee? 1 have no idea. One thing for sure, however, is that henceforth it will be a lot more iffy and less profitable to invest in high-risk ventures than to buy shares in very stable no-risk companies because dividend payments will be taxed at lower rates than riskier deals involving capital gains, particularly when such investments prove to be very worthwhile and very profitable.
Mr. Speaker, this is why 1 believe the whole question of capital gains taxation has to be reconsidered. For example, as I said earlier we operate under a system where a once-in-a-lifetime $100,000 capital gains tax exemption is allowed. After that, three quarters of any amount in excess of the limit will be taxed at rates higher that those applicable to dividends. This sounds totally irrational to me. I would suggest that the $100,000 exemption is nothing more than a band-aid approach and an election gimmick, not a sound tax policy under which income is taxed on the same basis-be it capital gain or dividend or interest income-which is the objective the Carter Commission was aiming at. Once again, that is why we Liberals, as 1 have said in the Finance Committee with the concurrence of other Members of that committe, suggest that capital gains be taxed 100 percent, but with an indexation formula which would eliminate gains due to inflation, so that real gains would be taxed at the taxpayers' marginal rate. In that case, we should also change the present dividend taxation formula to ensure that taxation rates would be the same for interest and dividend income, etc.
Mr. Speaker, I want to conclude my remarks by saying that the Conservative Government did not give us a tax reform that is fair to low and middle income Canadians. I said earlier that the net result of four years of this Conservative Government, tax reform included, is that the middle income taxpayer with two children will have to pay $1,200 more each year in taxes while the person who earning over $100,000 will pay $3,500 less. If that is what the Conservative Government and the Conservative Prime Minister call tax equity and social justice, I do not want to have anything to do with that kind of justice.
Yesterday, we were told that the Government could not afford greater tax fairness. It cannot index the child tax credit, it cannot index the disability tax credit, it cannot make tax credits refundable for low income people, because it does not have enough money. Mr. Speaker, how come the Government does not have enough money to bring more fairness to the tax system while it has plenty of money to make all kinds of preelection promises such as those we hear about day after day.
I do not understand why the Government does not have money for fiscal equity, but it does have money for all sorts of promises that it is announcing day after day which will cost a lot of money.

I read an article on Tory spending in The Toronto Star on August 6, written by Carol Goar, entitled: "Tory spree hits $14 billion". When one reads the article, one realizes that in the month of June the Government announced $5 billion of new spending. If that is added to the other announcements made since that date, the total reached the amount of $14 billion. Why does the Government have money for those things, including nuclear submarines and many other types of new spending? The amazing thing is that all those announcements are for the coming year. They will not affect this fiscal year but will affect the fiscal year after the general election. The Government is announcing new spending. It states that it will not affect the deficit and will not affect the public debt, but it will be spent over the coming five, six, seven years. Somewhere, some day, some how, some taxpayers will have to foot the bill.
That is why I am suggesting that, under the Tory administration, the financial decisions made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) are contrary to the speeches he was delivering before the election in 1984. Since the Tory Government has been in power the public debt has increased from $176 billion to more than $300 billion. That is over 40 per cent in four years. The Tory Government has added more debt to the public in four years than the Governments of the last generation.
Without the huge increase in taxes, the deficit under this Government would be around $36 billion or $37 billion. We recognize that the world economy has been very good over the last five or six years. This recovery started before the Tories took over power. If we consider the real numbers, taking into account the good economic conditions in the industrial world for the last five or six years, and taking into account the situation in this country, the deficit would be $36 billion or $37 billion without those huge tax increases.
What would be the situation if we had to face another economic crisis of the type that Canada had in 1980-1981 and the beginning of 1982? That crisis did not only occur in Canada. It was the same in the United States, Europe, and Japan. It was a world-wide crisis. If, in 1989-90 we have to suffer a similar crisis, and the rate of growth of the economy instead of being 2.8 per cent to 3 per cent comes down to 1 per cent, .5 per cent, or even minus 1 per cent, as we faced in the worst part of the crisis, how will we face the situation with the huge deficit that has been built by the Government during the years of prosperity?
It is a question that all taxpayers will have to study very carefully and be in a position to tell the Government, when the time comes, that the Tories have not met their promises, and that the Minister of Finance, instead of managing the deficit with a better managing of the expenditure side, has succeeded in cutting the deficit only by huge tax increases. This is contrary to the promises, and this is why the Government will be defeated when it has the courage to call a general election.

August 26, 1988
